summary: OpenManus funnels every agent, flow and tool through one AsyncOpenAI client in app/llm.py, whose three methods (ask, ask_with_images, ask_tool) are the app's five production LLM calls. The vendored router_runtime transport now sits under that client, so each request is planned individually: a Router catalog model goes to Router's /v1/responses with the Chat Completions call translated, and anything else -- a model Router doesn't list, an Azure deployment, a local Ollama build -- goes to the configured endpoint exactly as before. Because OpenManus points that one client at whatever endpoint config.toml names (OpenAI, Anthropic's compatible endpoint, Google, Jiekou.AI, PPIO, localhost), the wrap also unlocks the configured host, while never unlocking loopback or private addresses. Nothing changes until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set. All three methods were then driven against the local simulator and against live Router on both the OpenAI and the Anthropic-compatible host: 7 of 7 requests arrived, 200 each, and the existing test suite still passes unchanged. The Bedrock client (boto3 converse), the Azure client and the chart tool's Node subprocess stay where they are, for reasons given per item.
reviewed: The review looked at what this product actually spends on: a ReAct loop that re-sends an identical system prompt, tool schema set and growing history on every step (up to 20 steps per run, up to 15k characters of tool output per observation), a planning flow that makes two more calls per run, and a browser path that carries a screenshot per step. It measured the Router levers that apply to that shape on live Router (prompt caching, model tiers, the switchyard auto-router), read the agent loop for calls that are retried when they cannot succeed or sent with parameters the model rejects, and checked which configuration the code claims to support but never reads. Four improvements are built and tested; eight more are proposed, each either depending on a deployment's own primary model or changing what the model sees in a way no offline check can judge.

calls.model: configurable: [llm].model, passed to the Node subprocess

items.title: Route the one OpenAI client every agent shares
items.summary: The runtime transport goes under the AsyncOpenAI client in app/llm.py, so ask, ask_with_images and ask_tool reach Router for any catalog model.
items.gains: One key and one spend view for every agent, flow and tool in the app; per-request planning, so a model Router cannot serve still reaches the configured endpoint; the Router levers (caching, labels, tiers, fallbacks, timeouts) become available to this codebase through router.policy.json; Chat Completions is translated to Responses, which is the only surface Router serves for this SDK.
items.loses: OpenManus aims one OpenAI-compatible client at whatever endpoint config.toml names, so the wrap unlocks that host: on a reseller or compatible endpoint (Anthropic's /v1 compatible endpoint, Jiekou.AI, PPIO) a request whose model name happens to be a Router catalog id now goes to Router's own provider for that model instead of to the reseller, which can change price and, for open-weight ids, which provider's weights answer. Requests for any other model still go to the configured endpoint untouched, and loopback and private addresses are never unlocked, so a local Ollama deployment is unaffected. A translation layer is now in the request path.
items.price: The catalog price of the model the code names, now billed through Router instead of the configured vendor; no model or parameter changed.
items.why: Every LLM call in this repo that the scanner can see, plus every call it cannot (the agents build their clients through the LLM singleton), passes through the same constructor, so one wrap covers the whole product and nothing else needs touching. Routing per request rather than per client is what makes it safe here: this app's model is operator configuration, and a config that names a model Router does not list keeps working exactly as before rather than failing. If the host unlock is unwanted, dropping the unlock_hosts argument at app/llm.py:256 leaves only api.openai.com routed.

evidence.detail: A probe driving ask, ask (streaming), ask_with_images and ask_tool on gpt-4o-mini via api.openai.com and claude-haiku-4-5 via api.anthropic.com: 7 of 7 requests reached router-sim as POST /v1/responses, all valid, labelled app/llm.py:ask / ask_tool / ask_with_images.

The same probe against live Router with the migration key: 7 of 7 requests 200, x-router-provider openai for the gpt-4o-mini calls and anthropic for the claude-haiku-4-5 calls, including the image call.
mkdir ... && python -m compileall app protocol main.py ... && python -m pytest tests/ --ignore=tests/sandbox: 4 passed, unchanged from the baseline of 4.

router-migrate check --all: 5 of 7 scanner-visible calls now route; the two that do not are the Bedrock sites (item s1). With ROUTER_MIGRATE_TRACE on, a localhost Ollama config and a claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219 config both record to=provider, the latter with reason "model is not in the Router catalog" (item d1).

items.title: Bedrock keeps talking to Bedrock
items.summary: app/bedrock.py speaks to bedrock-runtime through boto3's converse API, which the runtime does not intercept and Router does not serve with the shared key.
items.loses: LLM traffic from Bedrock deployments is not on Router: it is billed to AWS and does not appear in Router's spend views.
items.why: This is a hand-written OpenAI-shaped shim over boto3, not an HTTP SDK the runtime can sit under, and the catalog's Bedrock ids are marked requires_byok, so Router would need the caller's own AWS credentials to serve them. Item p4 proposes retiring this path instead of routing it.

evidence.detail: router-migrate check --all reports both sites as "kept: other SDK / endpoint; Router does not serve this vendor's endpoint with the shared key".

items.title: Azure deployments keep their deployment endpoint
items.summary: The AsyncAzureOpenAI client built at app/llm.py:250 is left on Azure by the runtime, by design.
items.gains: an Azure-configured deployment behaves exactly as before, key and endpoint included
items.loses: Azure deployments get none of Router: their traffic is billed to Azure and is absent from Router's spend views.
items.why: The runtime refuses Azure clients because an Azure deployment name is not a Router catalog id and the request shape is Azure's. An Azure deployment that wants Router changes config.toml to the plain OpenAI path with a catalog model; nothing in the code needs to change for that.

evidence.detail: router_runtime.wrap_openai() returns Azure clients untouched (_is_openai excludes AsyncAzureOpenAI); the scanner sees no call site bound to this client.

items.title: The chart tool's Node subprocess still calls the vendor
items.summary: DataVisualization hands base_url, model and api_key to `npx ts-node src/chartVisualize.ts`, which posts to <base_url>/chat/completions from Node.
items.gains: nothing changes for the data-analysis agent's charts
items.loses: This is the one piece of LLM traffic in the app that is not on Router: it keeps using the provider key, and its spend is invisible to Router. The scanner cannot see it either (it leaves the process as a subprocess argument).
items.why: Router serves no /v1/chat/completions endpoint (404, plain text), and vmind builds that URL itself from the base URL it is given, so pointing it at Router would break it. Putting it on Router needs the TypeScript runtime inside that subprocess, which is proposed as p7.

evidence.detail: app/tool/chart_visualization/data_visualization.py:228-232 passes self.llm.base_url / model / api_key into the subprocess; src/chartVisualize.ts:343 constructs `${baseUrl}/chat/completions` for VMind. ROUTER.md section 2: /v1/chat/completions returns 404 on Router.

items.title: Pick the catalog model for claude-3-7-sonnet deployments
items.summary: A deployment pinned to claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219 (the shipped example config) routes nothing, because that id is not in Router's catalog.
items.gains: Naming a catalog id (or mapping the old one in router.policy.json) is what puts such a deployment's traffic on Router at all; today it keeps every request on Anthropic and silently gets none of the gains above.
items.loses: A different model answers. claude-sonnet-4-5 is the nearest same-family catalog id by capability (tools, images, temperature all supported, $3/$15 per 1M); claude-sonnet-5 is cheaper ($2/$10) but rejects `temperature`, which this app sets to 0.0 for repeatability, so its agent loop would run at the provider default sampling unless item i2 is also taken.
items.price: claude-sonnet-4-5 $3/$15 per 1M, claude-sonnet-5 $2/$10, claude-haiku-5-5 $0.10/$0.50; the current pin is not priced by Router at all.
items.why: Only the operator knows whether this deployment's prompts were tuned against claude-3-7-sonnet and how much of a model change is acceptable, so the migration does not guess: the runtime keeps unknown models on the provider. The decision is a one-line config.toml edit (preferred) or a router.policy.json model_map entry if the config must keep the old name.

evidence.detail: With RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY set and model claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219, ROUTER_MIGRATE_TRACE records to=provider, reason "model 'claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219' is not in the Router catalog" for both ask and ask_tool; 0 requests reached router-sim.
router-migrate levers (live catalog, 2026-10-15): claude-sonnet-4-5 in $3 out $15, claude-sonnet-5 in $2 out $10 (temperature not supported), claude-haiku-5-5 in $0.10 out $0.50.

items.title: Cache the agent step's prefix and label spend
items.summary: router.policy.json puts prompt_cache_key on every Router-bound request and tags it product=openmanus.
items.gains: The agent loop re-sends the same system prompt, tool schemas and history prefix on every step; only the tail is new. Measured on live Router with this app's own step shape, the second identical-prefix call cost 50% less on gpt-4o-mini and 84% less on claude-haiku-4-5. A 20-step run pays the write once and reads the prefix 19 times. The product tag and the per-call-site key also make Router's spend views usable.
items.loses: The first call after a prefix changes costs about 22% more on Claude (the cache write at 1.25x input price), so a run with a prompt that changes every step pays a little more. Nothing functional changes: the policy only adds fields to Router-bound requests, so the provider path never sees them.
items.price: Lower from the second step of every run: measured -50% (gpt-4o-mini) to -84% (claude-haiku-4-5) on a 4.2k-token prefix; +22% on the first Claude call.
items.why: This is the one lever whose value scales with exactly what this product does -- a long tool-calling loop over a fixed prompt -- and it needs no code change, only a committed policy file the runtime reads. The measurement also corrected an assumption worth recording: without prompt_cache_key neither model cached at all on Router's Responses surface (two identical calls, cached_tokens 0 both times), so this is the whole saving rather than a routing hint.

evidence.detail: Two identical calls per arm, 4.2k-token prefix + 5 tool schemas, live Router: claude-haiku-4-5 without a key $0.004591 then $0.004591 (cached 0, 0); with a key $0.005593 then $0.000745 (cached 4216). gpt-4o-mini without a key $0.000525 then $0.000530 (cached 0, 0); with a key $0.000508 then $0.000266 (cached 3200).
The compiled policy applied to a translated agent-step body puts prompt_cache_key=<label> and metadata {feature, product} on the request; the 7-call probe reached router-sim with 7 valid requests.
4 passed, unchanged.

items.title: Ask the catalog what a model can do, not a 2024 list
items.summary: Image support, temperature support and the output-cap parameter come from the Router catalog instead of two frozen model lists.
items.gains: Fixes the vision path on every current model: format_messages() silently dropped base64 screenshots for any model not in a six-entry list, and ask_with_images() refused outright. Verified on live Router, claude-sonnet-5 and gpt-5.4-mini now complete image calls that failed before any request was made. It also stops sending `temperature` to the 36 catalog ids that return 400 for it, and stops sending max_completion_tokens to Claude.
items.loses: On models the catalog says reject temperature (gpt-5.x, claude-sonnet-5, opus-4.7 and later, every *-5-5, Fable), the app's temperature=0.0 is no longer sent, so those models sample at their own default: less repeatable than the operator asked for, where before the request would have been refused by Router or the provider. Models the catalog does not know (a local Ollama build, a reseller's private id) keep exactly today's behaviour from the two lists.
items.price: no change, except that calls which used to fail now actually run (and cost) on vision models.
items.why: The two lists are a snapshot that the product has outgrown, and both failure modes are silent: an agent that takes a screenshot every step gets none of them through to a modern model, which looks like the model being bad at browsing rather than a dropped attachment. The catalog vendored with the runtime already answers these questions for every model Router serves, and keeping the lists as the fallback means no deployment loses behaviour it has today.

evidence.detail: Probe driving all three methods on claude-sonnet-5 and gpt-5.4-mini: 8 of 8 requests 200 after the change, including both image calls. Before the change the same probe got 6 of 8 out and exited 1, with "Model gpt-5.4-mini does not support images" raised locally.
6 new tests in tests/test_model_capabilities.py (catalog hits, dated-id resolution, text-only refusal, unknown-model fallback, temperature and max_completion_tokens rules); suite 4 -> 10 passed.

items.title: Give each agent its own model and its own label
items.summary: [llm.<agent>] sections are read at last, and each call is labelled <config>:<method> for Router.
items.gains: Two things that were advertised and absent. BaseAgent's llm field defaulted to LLM(), which is a valid LLM for the "default" config, so the validator's LLM(config_name=self.name) branch never ran and [llm.manus], [llm.browser], [llm.data_analysis] were dead config; the same dead branch is in ReActAgent and the DataVisualization tool. And every request reached Router labelled app/llm.py:ask_tool, because the runtime labels a call by the first frame in our code -- always that file -- so no agent could be told from another in spend views or targeted by router.policy.json. Real agents now arrive as manus:ask_tool, swe:ask_tool, data_analysis:ask_tool, planning:ask. This is the prerequisite for per-agent tiers, timeouts and cache keys (p1, p2, p3, p8).
items.loses: A deployment that already wrote an [llm.manus] or [llm.browser] section now gets it, where before it was ignored: that is the point, but it is a behaviour change for those config files. The planning flow asks for [llm.planning] and falls back to [llm] when absent. One extra request header per call when Router is not in use.
items.price: no change by itself; it is what makes a cheaper model per agent possible to configure at all.
items.why: Spend you cannot attribute is spend you cannot manage, and this product's whole cost profile is one agent's loop. The label is also the prompt cache key under i1, so per-agent labels give each agent its own cache affinity instead of one shared key.

evidence.detail: Three real ToolCallAgents driven one step each plus a planning-flow summary: 4 of 4 requests 200 on live Router, labelled manus:ask_tool, swe:ask_tool, data_analysis:ask_tool, planning:ask (same four labels against router-sim).

6 new tests in tests/test_per_agent_llm.py (per-agent section picked up, fallback to [llm], caller-supplied LLM still wins, planning flow asks for [llm.planning], label shape, caller label wins); suite 4 -> 10 passed.

items.title: Stop retrying calls that can never succeed
items.summary: The retry predicate keeps 429, 5xx, timeouts and connection errors and gives up at once on 4xx and on TokenLimitExceeded.
items.gains: All three methods retried `(OpenAIError, Exception, ValueError)` -- every exception there is -- six times with up to 60s of backoff. Measured on live Router, one call with an unusable image cost 6 Router requests (all 400) and 6 provider fallbacks; after the change, 1 and 1. A token-limit refusal, which is raised before any request is made, used to idle the agent for minutes of backoff before finishing. ToolCallAgent.think() now also recognises a bare TokenLimitExceeded, so an exhausted agent still finishes gracefully.
items.loses: A 4xx that would have succeeded on a later attempt -- a provider briefly returning 400 for a valid request -- now surfaces to the caller immediately instead of being retried. 429, 5xx, timeouts and transport errors are unaffected.
items.price: Up to 6x less spend on any call that fails with a 4xx, and no wasted provider-fallback calls behind them.
items.why: A 20-step agent run is a long thing to leave sitting in exponential backoff over a request the provider has already refused on its merits, and through Router each doomed attempt is charged twice (Router, then the runtime's provider fallback). The list of non-retryable statuses is deliberately short and conservative.

evidence.detail: Same probe with one unusable image: 6 requests to Router (all 400) on the migration branch, 1 request on this branch.

10 new tests in tests/test_llm_retry.py (TokenLimitExceeded, each non-retryable status, 429/5xx/connection/empty-response still retried, and a 400 reaching the client exactly once); suite 4 -> 14 passed.

items.title: Let Router pick the model for each agent step
items.summary: Point the agent loop at Router's `switchyard` id (or the account's auto-routing strategy) instead of one fixed model.
items.gains: On the same OpenManus step (4 tool schemas, a real task, 700-token prompt) measured on live Router: claude-sonnet-5 $0.003184, claude-haiku-5-5 about $0.00024, switchyard $0.000109 -- 29x cheaper than sonnet-5 -- and switchyard's four samples all produced a well-formed python_execute call with correct code, served by gpt-5.6-luna. An agent loop is exactly the heterogeneous workload per-request routing is for: most steps are bookkeeping, a few need the strong model.
items.loses: The model answering a step is no longer the one the operator configured, and can differ between steps of one conversation: prompts tuned to a specific model, and any evaluation baseline, stop being comparable. Router's choice is not contractual -- nothing in the measured facts guarantees a capability floor per request, and four samples of one step shape are not a quality measurement. Spend becomes harder to predict per run even though it was far lower here.
items.price: $0.000109 vs $0.003184 per step on the measured sample (-97%); unmeasured for other step shapes.
items.why: This is the largest cost lever found, and it is a one-line model change rather than a code redesign -- but it hands model choice to Router, which is a product decision about output quality that belongs to a human, not to this migration. Worth a side-by-side run of a few real tasks before adopting.

evidence.detail: 4 switchyard calls on one OpenManus step shape: all 200, all served by gpt-5.6-luna (provider openai), all emitting a correct python_execute call; first sample usage.cost $0.00010868 against claude-sonnet-5 $0.003184 and gpt-5.4-nano $0.0000553 (which produced no tool call at all).
No quality comparison over real OpenManus tasks; n=4 on a single step.

items.title: Run steps on a cheap model, escalate when it stalls
items.summary: Take each step on a cheap catalog model and re-take it on the strong model when the agent produces no tool call, malformed arguments, or repeats itself.
items.gains: Most steps in a run are mechanical (read a file, run a command, terminate) and the loop already has a stall detector (BaseAgent.is_stuck) whose only current response is to append a nudge. Spending the strong model's price only on the steps that need it is the structural version of p1's saving: claude-haiku-5-5 is $0.10/$0.50 against claude-sonnet-5's $2/$10, a 20x gap, and i3 makes the per-agent model configurable.
items.loses: Two models in one conversation (Router replays history across vendors, measured) and a retried step costs both. A cheap model that produces plausible-but-wrong tool calls does not look stuck, so escalation will miss cases a human would catch; agent runs become harder to reproduce. The escalation rule itself is new behaviour that needs a task suite to tune.
items.price: Up to ~20x less per routine step, plus the strong model's price on escalated steps.
items.why: It is the right shape for an agent loop and it uses machinery the loop already has, but the trigger ('did the cheap model do something useful?') is a quality judgement, and the measured sample already shows the trap: at a 300-token output cap claude-haiku-5-5 emitted a tool call with empty arguments and was cut off mid-reasoning; with 2,000 tokens it produced correct code. A cheap-first loop needs the output cap and the escalation rule tuned together.

evidence.detail: claude-haiku-5-5 on the same step: with max_output_tokens 300 it hit the cap and emitted python_execute with args "{}"; with 2,000 it emitted correct code. Cost about $0.00024 against claude-sonnet-5's $0.003184.
No run-level comparison of completion quality between tiers.

items.title: Fall back and cap provider time for the agent step
items.summary: Add fallbacks and provider_timeout for the agent-step label in router.policy.json.
items.gains: A 20-step run currently dies on the first step whose provider is down, and each step may sit for the 300s the SDK is given. A provider_timeout of 60-120s on the step label turns a stalled provider into a prompt 504 the loop can retry, and a fallback candidate keeps a run alive through a model being unavailable (measured: Router falls through a missing model, a 403 and an invalid parameter silently).
items.loses: A different, possibly weaker model answers some steps without saying so (the response does not name which candidate failed), and the least capable candidate limits tools and context for the whole request. Flex is ignored when a models list is present. A valid but slow call now fails at the timeout. Candidates must be chosen per deployment: the capability guard drops any candidate that cannot take the request's temperature, which is sent on every step here.
items.price: The serving candidate's price when a fallback serves; no change otherwise.
items.why: Left proposed rather than built because the candidate list depends on the deployment's primary model and on which agents are interactive -- both facts the operator has and this session does not. The policy edit is two keys under the agent-step label once that is decided.

evidence.detail: ROUTER.md 6.2/6.5: fallbacks are Responses-only, up to 15 candidates, silent fall-through on missing model / 403 / invalid parameter, cross-vendor works; provider_timeout max 660s, a timeout returns a plain-text 504. Fallback on real provider outages is documented but not measured.
Not built; no candidate list to check.

items.title: Retire app/bedrock.py and serve those deployments from Router
items.summary: Delete the 334-line boto3 shim and have api_type = "aws" deployments name a catalog model through the Router path.
items.gains: Removes a hand-written OpenAI-shaped translation layer with real defects: a module-global CURRENT_TOOLUSE_ID shared across all calls (two concurrent agents overwrite each other's tool-use ids), only the last system message survives, tool results are matched to whatever id was seen last, empty content is replaced with ".", and the streaming path indexes content blocks 0 and 1 by hand. All of it exists to make Bedrock look like chat.completions -- which is what Router does properly, for Claude and OpenAI models, on one key.
items.loses: Bedrock's own billing, quota and data-residency story goes away for those deployments: usage moves to Router's providers unless they configure Router's BYOK Bedrock ids with their own AWS credentials. Anyone depending on a Bedrock-only model id, an AWS commitment or in-region inference has to opt out. This deletes a supported configuration path, so it is a product decision, not a cleanup.
items.price: Catalog prices via Router (claude-sonnet-5 $2/$10) against the Bedrock ids' own ($2.20/$11 for us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5 in the catalog's BYOK rows).
items.why: Two of the seven call sites in this repo are in this file, it is the only remaining vendor glue, and its concurrency bug is the kind that produces mismatched tool results rather than an error. But removing a deployment option affects users, so it needs an owner's decision and a deprecation note, not a quiet migration.

evidence.detail: app/bedrock.py:13 declares CURRENT_TOOLUSE_ID as a module global mutated at lines 114, 149 and 279; _convert_openai_messages_to_bedrock_format keeps only the last system message (line 92) and reads the global for every tool result (line 123). Catalog: Bedrock ids are requires_byok.

items.title: Keep one screenshot in the browser agent's history
items.summary: Drop or downscale earlier base64 screenshots when a new one arrives, instead of re-sending every screenshot every step.
items.gains: The browser path adds a screenshot to memory on each step (toolcall.act() for any tool result carrying one, plus BrowserContextHelper), and every step re-sends all of them. At the counter's own numbers a full-detail screenshot is about 1,024-1,105 tokens, so by step 10 roughly 10k tokens of stale images ride along on every request, and on Claude image parts are not cache-discounted below the prefix that changed.
items.loses: The model can no longer compare the current page with earlier ones, which some browsing tasks need. Pruning the middle of the history also invalidates the cached prefix from that point (i1), so each prune costs one cache write.
items.price: Roughly 1,000 tokens per dropped image per subsequent step; on claude-sonnet-5 input that is about $0.002 per 1,000 tokens.
items.why: This is the biggest token sink in the vision path, but what the agent needs to see is a product judgement -- and the right fix may be to keep a low-detail thumbnail rather than nothing. Worth measuring against real browsing tasks first.

evidence.detail: app/agent/toolcall.py:act() appends a user message carrying base64_image for every tool result that has one, and nothing ever removes it; TokenCounter.count_image returns 1024 for the default detail and 1105 for a 1024x1024 high-detail image.

items.title: Send the next-step nudge without storing it
items.summary: ToolCallAgent.think() appends next_step_prompt to memory every step; send it with the request instead of keeping every copy.
items.gains: By step N the history holds N copies of the same instruction block (Manus's is a few hundred tokens), re-sent on every later request: quadratic waste in the loop's hottest call, and a history that reads as if the user repeated themselves. The model still sees the nudge once, at the end of each request, which is where it matters.
items.loses: What the model sees changes: earlier copies of the reminder disappear from the conversation, and a model that was effectively being re-anchored several times may behave differently. The stuck-state handler, which prepends to next_step_prompt, then also appears once rather than accumulating.
items.price: A few hundred tokens per step per step elapsed; at 20 steps and 300 tokens, roughly 57k input tokens a run before caching.
items.why: Small, obviously wasteful, and a one-function change -- but it is a change to the prompt the model sees on every step of every run, and nothing offline can tell whether the repetition was load-bearing. Cheap to A/B on a task suite.

evidence.detail: app/agent/toolcall.py:41-43 adds Message.user_message(self.next_step_prompt) to self.messages at the top of every think().

items.title: Put the chart tool's Node LLM call on Router
items.summary: Vendor routerRuntime.ts into app/tool/chart_visualization and wrap fetch in chartVisualize.ts before VMind is constructed.
items.gains: Closes the last unrouted LLM call in the app (item s3): chart and insight generation would be billed on the Router key, appear in spend views under its own label, and stop needing a provider key in the subprocess environment. The runtime translates the chat/completions call VMind makes into Responses, which is the shape Router serves.
items.loses: Adds a vendored TypeScript runtime and a fetch wrapper to a subprocess that runs through `npx ts-node`, so it cannot be verified without installing the chart tool's npm dependencies; the TS runtime's stack-derived labels are meaningless after bundling, so the label has to be set explicitly. If VMind sends anything Router cannot serve, those requests stay on the provider as they do today.
items.price: Catalog price through Router instead of the provider's; no model change.
items.why: Correct and in scope, but unverifiable in this session: the chart tool's node_modules are not installed and the path needs a live run to prove. Proposed so it can be built where the Node toolchain is available.

evidence.detail: The chart tool's npm dependencies (@visactor/vmind, ts-node, puppeteer) are not installed in this environment, so neither the current behaviour nor the wrapped behaviour could be exercised.

items.title: Summarise the finished plan on a cheap model, or not at all
items.summary: PlanningFlow._finalize_plan asks the main model to summarise a plan the app has already rendered; point [llm.planning] at a cheap model, or drop the call.
items.gains: The call takes a plan status block the app generates deterministically plus the step results and asks for prose. claude-haiku-5-5 at $0.10/$0.50 against claude-sonnet-5 at $2/$10 is a 20x cut on a pure summarisation with no tools, and i3 made [llm.planning] a real section, so it is config only. Dropping the call entirely is also defensible: _generate_plan_text_from_storage already produces a complete status report, and run_flow prints every step's result.
items.loses: A cheaper model writes a blander wrap-up; dropping the call removes the natural-language summary users see at the end of a flow run.
items.price: About $0.0003 instead of $0.007 for a typical 2k-in/300-out summary, or zero.
items.why: Easy money on a non-interactive call, but which of the two options is right depends on whether the summary is a feature anyone values -- an owner's call, and a one-line config change either way.

evidence.detail: router-migrate levers: claude-haiku-5-5 in $0.10 out $0.50; claude-sonnet-5 in $2 out $10. app/flow/planning.py:420 is the only ask() caller in the app.

items.title: The four built improvements apply together
items.summary: All four branches merge into the migration branch without conflicts, and the merged result passes tests and routes.
items.why: They touch the same file in places that are close together, so this was checked rather than assumed: a scratch merge of all four onto the migration branch was clean, the suite ran 26 passed (4 existing plus 22 added), and real agents driven through the merged code reached live Router with per-agent labels, the policy's cache key, and images working on claude-sonnet-5 and gpt-5.4-mini. One commit on the per-agent branch exists only to keep its helper out of the capability branch's way.

evidence.detail: Scratch merge of all four improvement branches onto router-migrate/migration: no conflicts; pytest tests/ --ignore=tests/sandbox with RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY set: 26 passed.

On the merged tree: 4 of 4 agent-step calls 200 (manus:ask_tool, swe:ask_tool, data_analysis:ask_tool, planning:ask) and 8 of 8 calls 200 across claude-sonnet-5 and gpt-5.4-mini including both image calls.

items.title: ask_with_images has no callers, and [llm.vision] is read by nothing
items.summary: The vision entry point and the vision config section are both unreachable; screenshots travel through ask_tool on the agent's own model.
items.why: Nothing in the repo calls LLM.ask_with_images, and nothing constructs LLM(config_name="vision"), yet every shipped example config defines [llm.vision] with a vision model -- so an operator who configures one is silently ignored, and images reach whichever model the agent itself uses (which, before i2, meant they were dropped unless that model was on a six-entry list). Both call sites were still migrated and verified, because the method is public API. Worth deciding later whether images should route to a vision-configured model (a natural use of Router's cross-vendor history replay) or whether the method and the config section should go.

evidence.detail: grep over app, protocol, main.py, run_*.py: no reference to ask_with_images outside app/llm.py and no LLM(config_name="vision"); config/config.example.toml and five of the model example configs define [llm.vision].
